You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 4.5 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 5.5 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 4.5 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 4.5 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.8 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 120 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 3300 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       3.33    3.36    49.3       -      5.05  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S2       3.18     3.2    44.2       -      10.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S3       7.08    7.13     110   0.209      5.01  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       2.21    2.22    33.8       -      1.04  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5        3.4    3.44    83.3       -       3.5  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       2.81    2.83    28.1       -       3.6  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 4.5 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 7 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

Design 1 'S-SECE': failed the screen and was not tuned (topology a814429d60b6).

what this means:
- with the output fixed at 4.5 V, the net power delivered covers only -23 % of the load's need on S2 (heavy load), -108 % of the load's need on S4 (weak excitation), -51 % of the load's need on S6 (Cp +20 %, hot) (best of the value presets tried)

REPEATED PROBLEM: your last three designs all show the same failure: too little power reaches the output on some conditions [underpower]. Change the part of the circuit responsible for it rather than its values.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor-node load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out\_min} \ge 4.5\text{V}$ (settled mean)
        *   $V_{out\_max} \le 5.5\text{V}$ (absolute max)
        *   Ripple $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$ (0.7-0.8s)
        *   Startup $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$ (time to reach 4.5V)
        *   Settled $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$ (|mean(0.7-0.8s) - mean(0.6-0.7s)|)
    *   Piezo: Sinusoidal current source $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25-30nF) and $R_{leak} = 20\text{M}\Omega$.
    *   Open circuit voltage amplitude: $V_{oc} = I_p / (2\pi f C_p) \approx 3.8\text{V}$ (for S1).
    *   Important: $V_{oc}$ (3.8V) is lower than the target $V_{out}$ (4.5-5.5V). This means a simple rectifier (FBR) will not work (as seen in reference design results). We need a voltage boost or a synchronized switching mechanism (like SSHI) to "pump" the voltage.

    *   `P-SSHI` (Parallel Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor):
        *   Score: 40.40.
        *   Passed S2, S6.
        *   S1: $V_{out\_max}$ (5.58V) slightly fails.
        *   S3: $V_{out\_max}$ (12.22V) fails badly, $dv$ fails.
        *   S4: $V_{out\_min}$ (3.77V) fails, $t_{up}$ fails.
        *   S5: $V_{out\_max}$ (6.10V) fails, $dv$ fails.
        *   Crucially, P-SSHI can deliver enough power (screen result: 2260% of needs on S4), but it doesn't regulate the output voltage. It's an open-loop converter.

    *   The problem with `P-SSHI` is voltage regulation ($V_{out\_max} \le 5.5\text{V}$) and stability/startup on the weakest condition (S4).
    *   Wait, the screen for `P-SSHI` says it delivers 97.4 uW on S4 when fixed at 4.5V, while the load needs 4.31 uW. So it *can* deliver enough power. Why did it settle at 3.77V? Likely because the SSHI efficiency or the rectifier stage is limiting it, or the storage capacitor is too small/large. Actually, the `P-SSHI` implementation used a full bridge (D1-D4) and an L-S inverter.
    *   The primary issue is that $V_{out}$ goes too high on S3/S5 and too low on S4. We need a way to clamp the voltage at 5.5V without wasting too much power or affecting the startup too much.
    *   A Zener diode (DZ33) only clamps at 3.3V, which is too low (target 4.5-5.5V). We can't use a single DZ33.
    *   What about a shunt regulator? Or a modified SSHI?
    *   Let's look at the P-SSHI again. It's essentially a rectifier with an inductor-switch in parallel with the piezo to flip the voltage.
    *   To prevent $V_{out}$ from exceeding 5.5V, we could use a Zener-based shunt, but 3.3V is too low. We could stack Zener diodes? No, the components list says DZ33 is a 3.3V Zener.
    *   Wait, we have a 5.5V limit. If we can't use a zener at 5.5V, how do we regulate?
    *   Wait, the prompt mentions "zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out... reverse-biased... breaks down at 3.3V)". This is an example. Maybe we can use a Zener in a different configuration? No, a Zener is just a Zener.
    *   Actually, the simplest way to limit the voltage in these harvesting circuits, if we don't have a programmable regulator, is to increase the load or use a shunt. But the load $R_L$ is fixed.
    *   Is there another way to regulate? We could use a "bleeder" resistor, but that wastes power and might make S4 fail. `P-SSHI-Bleed` failed miserably.
    *   Let's reconsider the SSHI. The `P-SSHI` failed $V_{out\_max}$ on S3 (12.22V). S3 is "strong excitation, light load" (Ip=120uA, RL=10kOhm). This is the "worst case" for overvoltage.

    *   The goal is $4.5 \text{V} \le V_{out} \le 5.5 \text{V}$.
    *   $V_{oc}$ is ~3.8V.
    *   In P-SSHI, the voltage flipping increases the effective $V_{oc}$ seen by the rectifier.
    *   If $V_{out}$ is too high, we need to dissipate energy.
    *   What if we use a Zener diode to clamp the *piezo* voltage before it hits the rectifier? No, that would waste the energy we are trying to harvest.
    *   What if we use a Zener in series with the output? No.
    *   Wait, the `P-SSHI` output $V_{max}$ on S1 was 5.58V. That's very close! Only S3 and S5 were significantly over.
    *   S3: $I_p = 120\text{uA}, R_L = 10\text{M}\Omega$.
    *   S5: $I_p = 50\text{uA}, R_L = 3.3\text{M}\Omega, f = 80\text{Hz}$.
    *   The `P-SSHI` is almost there. We just need to prevent the voltage from climbing too high on S3.

    *   Could we use a "crowbar" or a shunt? A Zener DZ33 (3.3V) is too low for the output.
    *   But what if we put the Zener on the *input* side? If the voltage across the piezo exceeds a certain value, it clamps. But the SSHI depends on the voltage reaching a peak.
    *   Actually, let's look at the components again: `DZ33 = 3.3 V zener`.
    *   What if we use a diode and a Zener in series?
        *   $V_{forward} (DSCH) \approx 0.25\text{V}$
        *   $V_{zener} (DZ33) \approx 3.3\text{V}$
        *   Total $\approx 3.55\text{V}$. Still too low.
    *   Wait, if we put two Zeners in series? $3.3 + 3.3 = 6.6\text{V}$. Too high.
    *   Wait, if we use a Zener and a silicon diode (DSI)? $3.3 + 0.5 = 3.8\text{V}$.
    *   Wait, if we use a Zener and a resistor? No.

    *   The `P-SSHI` failed $V_{out\_min}$ on S4 (3.77V).
    *   S4: $I_p = 40\text{uA}, f = 100\text{Hz}, C_p = 25\text{nF}, R_L = 4.7\text{M}\Omega$.
    *   The power available is $P \approx 0.5 \cdot C_p \cdot (2\pi f)^2 \cdot V_{oc}^2$.
    *   With SSHI, we can extract more.
    *   The `P-SSHI` was:
        `D1 D pzp out DSCH`
        `D2 D pzn out DSCH`
        `D3 D 0 pzp DSCH`
        `D4 D 0 pzn DSCH`
        `L1 L pzp n1 0.01`
        `S1 S n1 pzn ctrl=G1`
        `G1 SYNC ton=0.001s phase=0.00271 edges=both`
        `C1 C out 0 6.13e-07`
    *   This is a standard SSHI. The rectifier is a full bridge.
    *   Wait, the `P-SSHI` result says $V_{out\_min} = 3.77\text{V}$ on S4.
    *   Is it possible to increase the voltage on S4?
    *   Maybe a voltage doubler?
    *   The `Doubler-SSHI` and `Doubler-SSHI-Boost` were tried and failed (nan score). Let's look at why. Maybe the connectivity was wrong.
    *   A standard SSHI boosts the piezo voltage. A doubler (like a Greinacher circuit) would double the rectified voltage.
    *   If the P-SSHI gives 3.77V on S4, a doubler-SSHI might give ~7V, which would then be clamped.

    *   Let's try a different SSHI topology. Instead of a full bridge, what if we use a half-bridge or a different rectification?
    *   Actually, the P-SSHI is quite efficient. Let's try to improve the voltage regulation.
    *   Since we can't use a 5V Zener, maybe we can use a "leakage" path that becomes more conductive as the voltage rises?
    *   A Zener diode $DZ33$ in series with a resistor to ground?
        *   At $V_{out} = 4.5\text{V}$, $I_{bleed} = (4.5 - 3.3) / R = 1.2 / R$.
        *   At $V_{out} = 12\text{V}$, $I_{bleed} = (12 - 3.3) / R = 8.7 / R$.
        *   If we pick $R = 1\text{M}\Omega$:
            *   At 4.5V, $I = 1.2\text{uA}$.
            *   At 12V, $I = 8.7\text{uA}$.
            *   This is too small to stop the voltage from climbing to 12V on S3 ($R_L = 10\text{M}\Omega, I_{load} = 1.2\text{uA}$).
            *   Actually, if $R = 100\text{k}\Omega$, $I_{bleed}$ at 12V is $87\text{uA}$. That would definitely pull the voltage down.
            *   But at 4.5V, $I_{bleed} = 12\text{uA}$. The load $R_L$ on S4 is $4.7\text{M}\Omega$, so $I_{load} = 4.5 / 4.7\text{M} = 0.95\text{uA}$.
            *   $I_{bleed} (12\text{uA})$ is much larger than $I_{load} (0.95\text{uA})$, so it might prevent S4 from reaching 4.5V.
    *   Wait, what if the Zener is in series with a diode?
        *   `D_bleed` (DSCH, 0.25V) + `DZ33` (3.3V) + `R_bleed`.
        *   Total drop $\approx 3.55\text{V}$.
        *   Still, $I_{bleed}$ would start at $V_{out} = 3.55\text{V}$.

    *   The current `P-SSHI` is almost perfect for S1, S2, S6. It only fails $V_{out\_max}$ on S1, S3, S5.
    *   $V_{out\_max}$ S1: 5.58V (very close to 5.5V)
    *   $V_{out\_max}$ S3: 12.22V (far)
    *   $V_{out\_max}$ S5: 6.10V (close)
    *   And it fails $V_{out\_min}$ on S4 (3.77V).
    *   This suggests we need a slightly higher "gain" for S4 and a "clamp" for S3.
    *   If we use a slightly different SSHI (e.g., with a higher $L$), we might get more voltage on S4. But $L$ is already $0.01\text{H}$ (max).
    *   Wait, the `P-SSHI` had a $V_{out}$ of 3.77V on S4. If we can just lift that by 0.8V, and drop S3 by 6V...
    *   What if we use a different rectifier? A charge pump?
    *   Let's try a "Self-Synchronized" approach or a different switching phase.
    *   Actually, let's try to add a shunt regulator that only kicks in above 5V.
    *   Since we only have $DZ33$ (3.3V), how about we use two $DZ33$ in series?
        *   $3.3 + 3.3 = 6.6\text{V}$.
        *   If we put two $DZ33$ in series from `out` to `0`:
            *   Below 6.6V, they are off.
            *   Above 6.6V, they conduct.
            *   This would clamp S3 (12.22V) and S5 (6.10V - wait, 6.10V is below 6.6V).
            *   S1 (5.58V) is also below 6.6V.
            *   So two Zeners in series would clamp S3 to ~6.6V. This is still above 5.5V.
    *   What about two Zeners in series, but one is backward? No.
    *   What about a Zener in series with a diode? $3.3 + 0.25 = 3.55\text{V}$.
    *   What if we use the Zener as part of a voltage divider or a more complex shunt? No, too many components.

    *   Maybe the P-SSHI can be improved by changing the rectifier.
    *   Current P-SSHI: Full bridge.
    *   What if we use a half-wave rectifier? No, that's less efficient.
    *   What if we use a "voltage doubler" as the rectifier?
    *   A standard voltage doubler (Greinacher) consists of two diodes and two capacitors.
    *   `pzp` -> `D1` -> `n1`
    *   `n1` -> `C1` -> `0`
    *   `pzn` -> `D2` -> `out`
